The Starry Night

Vincent van Gogh, 1889

Oil on canvas

Swirling night sky in deep blues and bright yellows, with thick, rhythmic brushstrokes.

Use this style

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night, 1889. Museum of Modern Art, New York. Source on Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

About the painting

Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself after a breakdown. The view is the one from his east-facing window before sunrise, but the village is largely invented and the cypress is pulled up close so that it rises like a flame against the sky.

Everything is made of short, loaded strokes laid side by side: ultramarine and cobalt in the sky, chrome yellow in the stars and moon, and the large spiral at the centre that gives the painting its movement. The Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired it in 1941.

How it looks on your photo

The model takes the dark blue and the yellow highlights, and turns flat areas such as skies and water into curving strokes. Landscapes and night scenes work best. On close-up faces the effect can be heavy, so try an intensity around 50 to 60%.
